title: Phaedo
author: Plato
openingText: ECHECRATES: Were you there yourself, Phaedo, in the prison with Socrates on the day he drank the poison?
about:
Socrates is in prison, and the sacred ship whose voyage delayed his execution has returned. His friends gather for his final day. Instead of avoiding the subject of death, he asks what happens to the soul and whether philosophy prepares a person to face it.

Phaedo recounts the conversation to Echecrates, who was not there. Socrates develops several arguments for the soul's survival. Simmias and Cebes challenge him: could the soul disappear like the harmony of a broken instrument, or wear out after surviving many bodies? Their objections make the conversation a test of reasons as well as a scene of friendship and grief.

The dialogue moves between close argument, a mythical account of the afterlife, and the practical details of Socrates' death. These passages do not all claim the same kind of certainty. Read for the distinctions between what a speaker thinks has been proved, what still troubles him, and what he hopes may be true.

angleCards.title: Follow the arguments
angleCards.text: Trace each argument for the soul's survival and identify the assumptions it needs.
angleCards.angleObjective: Help me follow the arguments in Phaedo, distinguish their premises from their conclusions, and test the objections without assuming that the conclusions are true.

angleCards.title: Listen to the objections
angleCards.text: Simmias compares the soul to a harmony; Cebes compares it to a weaver who outlasts several cloaks. What does each comparison challenge?
angleCards.angleObjective: Help me understand the different objections raised by Simmias and Cebes and evaluate whether Socrates answers each one.

angleCards.title: Philosophy and living
angleCards.text: Socrates describes philosophy as preparation for death. How does that shape his account of knowledge, pleasure and conduct?
angleCards.angleObjective: Help me examine what Socrates' account of philosophy implies for everyday life, while distinguishing his claims from advice I must accept.

angleCards.title: Read the final scene
angleCards.text: Watch how argument gives way to farewells, grief and small practical actions.
angleCards.angleObjective: Help me read the final scene closely, attending to narration, gestures and dialogue while distinguishing textual evidence from interpretations of Plato's intentions.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: He leads the conversation in prison, argues for the soul's immortality, welcomes objections and prepares to drink the poison.

cast.name: Phaedo
cast.description: He was present in the prison and tells Echecrates what happened. His account includes both the arguments and his own mixed feelings of pleasure and grief.

cast.name: Cebes
cast.description: He accepts that the soul may have existed before birth but questions whether it must survive forever. His weaver analogy distinguishes lasting longer from being indestructible.

cast.name: Simmias
cast.description: He suggests that the soul might depend on the body as a harmony depends on an instrument. Even after the replies, the difficulty of the subject leaves him cautious.

cast.name: Crito
cast.description: He helps with arrangements, asks about Socrates' wishes and burial, and promises to pay the final debt to Asclepius.

cast.name: Echecrates
cast.description: He asks Phaedo to recount the death and reacts to the arguments as the story unfolds. His questions form the dialogue's outer frame.

whyItMatters.title: Different claims need different proofs
whyItMatters.body: Showing that the soul existed before birth is not yet showing that it survives death. Showing that it lasts longer than a body is not yet showing that it can never perish. The dialogue makes these differences explicit through its objections.

whyItMatters.title: Keep questioning without giving up
whyItMatters.body: When apparently strong arguments collapse, the listeners begin to distrust reasoning itself. Socrates warns them against this response and asks them to examine their own skill at judging arguments.

whyItMatters.title: Proof, hope and grief
whyItMatters.body: Simmias compares a human explanation to a raft for navigating life. Later, Socrates cautions against insisting that his description of the afterlife is exactly true. The final scene places these questions beside the friends' grief and Socrates' composure.
